title: ML Multi-Factor Cross-Sectional with Upstream Contamination Bias Correction on H198 Universe
source: arXiv:2507.07107 (Jul 2025) — "Machine Learning Enhanced Multi-Factor Quantitative Trading: A Cross-Sectional Portfolio Optimization Approach with Bias Correction" (Du)
description: Apply the paper's bias-correction methodology to the H198 NASDAQ 30-stock universe. Key insight: rolling-window factor pipelines suffer 'upstream contamination' when price-limit or stale-price observations are ingested before filtering — inflating apparent IC by 18% and reducing realized Sharpe by 0.44 points. The paper's fix: tensor-based factor computation with contamination flags, GBM data augmentation for thin trading days, and cross-sectional neutralization. Port to US large-cap equities (different bias profile: no price limits, but earnings blackout windows and ex-dividend date contamination apply). Validated on Chinese A-shares Sharpe > 2.0; adaptation to US expected to yield more modest gains but addresses real biases in our H198 pipeline.
content_summary: Paper by Yimin Du presents: (1) Upstream contamination bias: daily returns computed from non-executable closing prices (China price limits → ~3% of observations) inflate IC by 18% and reduce Sharpe 0.44 points. Fix: flag and exclude contaminated price observations before factor computation. US analog: ex-dividend date price drops, corporate action adjustments, earnings halt days. (2) 500-1000 factor pipeline from alpha101 extensions + microstructure signals, computed via PyTorch tensor acceleration. (3) GBM data augmentation to handle thin-trading periods. (4) Cross-sectional neutralization (industry + size) reduces factor correlation and improves prediction stability. Results: 20% annualized return, Sharpe > 2.0 on A-shares 2010-2024. GitHub: github.com/initial-d/ml-quant-trading. US adaptation: apply contamination flags to (a) ex-dividend dates (yfinance adjusts prices but in-period raw return may spike), (b) stock split days, (c) earnings halt opens. Use H198's existing 30-stock universe with LightGBM ranker (H320 partial-confirmed) as the base model and add bias correction as preprocessing step.
variants: Var A: H198 6-1m momentum baseline with contamination-flagged returns (ex-div/split days excluded from signal)
Var B: Var A + LightGBM ranker on alpha101 subset (17 LASSO-surviving signals from H380) with bias correction
Var C: Var B + cross-sectional industry neutralization (GICS sector)
Var D: Var C + GBM data augmentation for thin-trading months (low ADV stocks)
Var E: H198 baseline (no bias correction) — sanity check
gate: OOS Sharpe > 1.174 (H198 baseline) AND MaxDD improvement >= 2pp
data_requirements: yfinance for H198 30-stock universe (NASDAQ large-cap). Alpha101 factors: already computed for H215 (alpha101-overlap.md). Ex-dividend dates: yfinance dividend history for contamination flagging. GICS sector: already built for H181 (sector-classification.md). LightGBM: already used in H320. Paper's GitHub: github.com/initial-d/ml-quant-trading (reference for factor engineering; not directly cloneable since China-focused).
implementation_notes: Contamination flagging for US: (1) compute raw daily returns; (2) flag days where |return| > 15% (likely corporate action or error) for exclusion from signal; (3) flag ex-dividend dates from yfinance dividend calendar — the return on ex-div date includes dividend component not from price momentum. Step 2 is the key novel contribution for US equities. Alpha101 factor selection: use the 17 LASSO-surviving signals from H380 (cross-market transfer paper) as the starting factor set — these are the signals that transfer from A-shares to US large-cap. LightGBM config: same hyperparams as H320 (n_estimators=200, max_depth=5, learning_rate=0.05, subsample=0.8). Cross-sectional neutralization: demean by GICS sector within each monthly cross-section before ranking. Expected challenge: US large-cap 30-stock universe has very thin cross-section for ML — high overfitting risk. Expand to H417 60-stock combined universe (Var B extension) if 30-stock fails.
